source.title: SONI: Selective Orthogonalisation via Noise Injection

record.file_problem: The supplied text runs from the title through the appendices, but many mathematical symbols and parameter values are missing or rendered blank.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses superposition as motivation for a new fine-tuning method and reports how that method changes feature geometry in toy models. It does not measure whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs or test whether superposition causes polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The reported outcomes concern targeted orthogonalisation and performance in Toy Models of Superposition, not mixed neuron responses. Rows record these geometry results as related findings, with versions set to none. The study explicitly says it has not applied SONI to LLMs or verified downstream interpretability or steering effects.
record.test_reason: The study treats superposition as a premise and reports only how its own fine-tuning method (SONI) changes feature-vector geometry in tied-weight TMS autoencoders. It never measures whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, across vision or language models. It also does not test whether superposition causes polysemanticity, or how architecture, measurement or training affect it.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SONI selectively orthogonalises a target feature in TMS models across dimensionalities with minimal performance cost. They also conclude it fails under feature co-activation above about 1 active feature per input, and it is untested on LLMs and on downstream safety tasks.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses targeted noise injection during fine-tuning of tied-weight TMS autoencoders; it does not reproduce neuron visualization or mixed-response analysis from the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on sparsity/co-activation, latent dimensionality, noise parameter sigma, and the orthogonality parameters discussed in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: Targeted directional noise during fine-tuning makes one chosen TMS feature nearly orthogonal to the others at n=5, 20, 400 and 1600. Performance cost is minimal. The method fails, with target collapse, when expected active features per input exceed about 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In TMS toy models, superposition geometry for a chosen feature can be selectively reduced by noise-injection fine-tuning, but only in sparse, low co-activation regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: Max cosine similarity is U-shaped in the noise strength sigma, while test error rises monotonically with sigma.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The degree of orthogonalisation and its performance cost under SONI depend on the noise strength chosen.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to toy models; the study has not tested LLMs or downstream interpretability and steering tasks. It reports no uncertainty estimates, and many numerical parameter values are missing from the supplied rendering.
record.rows_left_out: No further claim-related geometry results were omitted; plotted numeric values are not recoverable from the supplied text.

untested.parts: No image classifiers or neuron responses to image categories.
No transformer language model MLP neurons.
Uses superposition toy models but never links superposition to neurons responding to unrelated inputs. The TMS hidden space is a linear bottleneck with no privileged neuron basis.
No setting with enough neurons for every feature, and no test of whether initialization or noise causes polysemanticity. Implicit regularisation is mentioned only in relation to feature norms.
No share of polysemantic neurons is measured across activation functions, architectures or regularization.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong capstone post with no uncertainty estimates, and many parameter values are blank in the rendered text. The 'feature vectors' are columns of W in a linear-bottleneck autoencoder, not neuron activations, so the results cannot bear on neuron polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or neuron response to image categories is measured.
No transformer language model or MLP neuron responses to tokens or contexts are measured.
The study uses superposition toy models and discusses feature geometry, but does not test whether superposition causes neurons to respond to unrelated inputs.
No polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise in a network with sufficient neurons is measured.
No change in the share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization methods is measured.
No neuron explanations or shared features underlying purportedly mixed responses are examined.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons is made.
